extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (especially aesthetics and Kantian studies)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for forming and evaluating aesthetic judgements (judgements of taste), especially Kant's conditions for when a representation is judged beautiful. Focuses on the relation between feeling of pleasure, cognitive faculties, and concepts of purposiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgement of taste is aesthetical
rubrics_metrics.description: To decide whether anything is beautiful we refer the representation not by the Understanding to the Object for cognition but by the Imagination (perhaps in conjunction with the Understanding) to the subject, and its feeling of pleasure or pain. The determining ground of the judgement is subjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinguishes aesthetic judgements from logical/cognitive judgements: an aesthetical judgement refers representations to the subject (feeling) rather than to the object (knowledge). Example/explanation: apprehending a purposive building is different from being conscious of satisfaction in that representation. Aesthetical judgement adds nothing to cognition but compares the given representation with the whole faculty of representations insofar as the mind is conscious of its state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satisfaction determining judgement of taste is disinterested
rubrics_metrics.description: The satisfaction (interest) combined with a representation is disinterested when it is independent of any concern about the object's existence or any further use; in judging beauty we seek whether the mere representation is accompanied by satisfaction regardless of the object's existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disinterestedness means the pleasure is not tied to desire, possession, or pragmatic interest. Examples given: one may dislike a palace for moral or personal reasons yet still judge it beautiful if the mere representation yields pleasure; responses tied to desire or utility (e.g., liking cook-shops) do not count as aesthetic judgement. The judgement of beauty must be based on mere observation (intuition or reflection) with indifference to existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic pleasure is not cognitive or practical (not based on concepts or desire)
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasure that grounds a judgement of taste cannot be produced through concepts (cognition) nor through the faculty of desire (practical reason). It is a feeling bound up with the mere apprehension of form and cannot be reduced to conceptual determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic pleasure precedes and does not result from having a determinate concept of the object; it cannot be captured by conceptual predicates. It is empirically felt in reflection and therefore cannot establish objective necessity as a cognitive judgement would. The concept of purposiveness here has no reference to desire or practical purposiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure arises from harmony of cognitive faculties (purposiveness for the subject)
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasure of taste arises when the Imagination (faculty of intuition) is placed, by a representation of form, in harmonious accord with the Understanding (faculty of concepts), producing a feeling of pleasure—i.e., the form appears purposive for our cognitive faculties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the notion of a 'subjective formal purposiveness'—the object seems fitted to our cognitive faculties, producing pleasure without being subsumable under a concept. The feeling is immediate and indicates a purposiveness of the object in relation to the reflective judgement's need to find unity between intuition and concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgement of taste claims universal validity despite subjectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the judgement of taste is based on a subjective feeling, it nevertheless claims the agreement of everyone; the subject judges the pleasure as necessarily connected with the representation and therefore expects universal assent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant argues this claim is possible because the ground of the pleasure lies in the universal conditions of reflective judgement (the common structure of imagination and understanding). Example: a singular empirical observation (a drop of water in an ice-crystal) may rightly claim universal agreement because it is formed under universal conditions of possible experience; by analogy, a taste-judgement appeals to shared faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic (formal) purposiveness vs. teleological (objective) purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish two kinds of purposiveness: (1) Formal/subjective purposiveness (natural beauty) judged aesthetically by taste via feeling of pleasure; (2) Real/objective purposiveness (natural purposes/organisms) judged teleologically by concepts, Understanding and Reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural beauty presents the concept of formal purposiveness (presentation via feeling), whereas natural purposes present the concept of real purposiveness (presentation via concepts). The aesthetical judgement contributes to critique of the judging subject, while teleological judgement belongs to theoretical philosophy and attempts to judge objects under concepts of purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflective (not determinant) character of the judgement of taste
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgement of taste is a reflective judgement: it does not apply a pre-given concept to determine an object but seeks a concept for given particulars. It prescribes a principle for reflection (purposiveness) without determining objects a priori.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflective judgement is regulative: it assumes a principle a priori (purposiveness of nature for our cognitive faculties) to guide reflection in forming unity among diverse empirical laws, but it does not determine objects in the manner of determinant judgement. This is why aesthetic judgement can guide inquiry without providing cognitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feeling of pleasure in discovering unity (admiration) grounds aesthetic response
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovering that heterogeneous empirical laws or phenomena can be combined under one principle (a unity) produces a marked pleasure or admiration, which often continues even when familiar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This pleasure motivates reflective judgement to seek principles unifying diverse phenomena; if investigation suggested endless heterogeneity making unity impossible, this would displease. The pleasure is tied to the success of finding systematic unity and is distinct from mere cognitive recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transcendental principle of purposiveness for reflection on nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The Judgement presupposes a transcendental (a priori) principle that nature, though empirically contingent, is to be reflected upon as if it were purposive for our cognitive faculties—this is a subjective principle of judgement necessary for making connected experience possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle is not a constitutive natural law but a regulative maxim of the reflective judgement ('law of the specification of nature') that enables the Understanding to seek unity in empirical laws. It must be assumed a priori by the Judgement to carry out reflection and investigation, although it does not ascribe objective features to nature itself.
